findings.matters: A government write-off of most of an accrued DSG deficit is a major change in SEND funding exposure, and the unconfirmed treatment of future deficits remains a question for other councils with high needs deficits.

findings.matters: A ringfenced HRA reserve well above its floor shows the housing account can absorb cost pressures without drawing on the general fund.

findings.headline: Blackpool has granted £3.48m of medium-term cash flow loans to its wholly-owned companies
findings.detail: The paper says medium-term cash flow loans totalling £3.48m have been granted to the council's WOCs. It also states that there are currently no short-term cash flow loans outstanding in respect of council WOCs.
findings.matters: Cash flow lending to companies is a separate exposure from capital loans, and finance officers elsewhere will want to see how it is sized and whether short-term support is outstanding.

findings.detail: The paper says the council supports WOC capital spending where a business case shows either a valid spend-to-save initiative or an opportunity to generate income. The council's exposure to principal and capitalised interest on these loans is currently £57.94m.
findings.matters: This is the council's largest stated exposure to its companies in the paper, and it depends on the companies' income generating the returns the business cases assumed.
findings.figures: Exposure to principal and capitalised interest £57.94m

findings.detail: The Shareholder Committee authorised on 4 February 2025 a repayment period of up to 10 years for COVID recovery loans, after the initial 5-year term. The paper says the repayment period will be set case by case.
findings.matters: Extending maturities moves repayment of council lending to companies further out, which affects the council's cash flow and the risk on those loans.
findings.figures: Up to 10 years repayment period, following initial 5-year term; authorised 4 February 2025

findings.detail: The paper says the £24m Covid Recovery Fund, ringfenced for WOCs and set up in November 2020 with a 20% contingency, has loan approvals of £16.11m. Of this, £10.08m has been drawn and £4.90m has since been repaid. The Business Loans Fund Panel monitors progress against each company's recovery plan.
findings.matters: Repayment of recovery loans to the council depends on the companies meeting their plans, so the drawn and repaid figures show how much of the council's lending to companies is being returned.

findings.headline: CIPFA has advised Blackpool that WOC forecast losses are not included in the council's forecast revenue outturn
findings.detail: The paper says the council took CIPFA advice on the accounting treatment of company forecast losses. The advice is that the losses are not part of the forecast revenue outturn and will instead appear in the council's consolidated financial position.

findings.matters: A forecast loss in council-owned companies can sit outside the council's revenue outturn, so finance directors and lenders need to see it alongside the council's own position.

findings.quote: judged Blackpool’s Childrens Social Care service to be Outstanding

findings.matters: Agency staff costs are a common pressure on children's services budgets, so a finance director elsewhere can compare this agency rate and its reduction over time with their own.

findings.matters: Councils that budgeted for Bank of England rate cuts in 2026/27 face the same exposure in their treasury lines if those cuts do not arrive, so this is a direct read-across for their own interest assumptions.

findings.matters: Moving revenue-funded vehicle costs onto prudential borrowing to produce an in-year underspend increases the council's borrowing requirement and its future revenue cost of capital.

findings.detail: The paper says savings have been identified within the funding of replacement equipment, and the capitalisation of that equipment is forecast to contribute the saving. This moves the cost from the revenue budget to capital.

findings.figures: 11th lowest in the country; 65% of rents set below formula rents; CPI +1; currently 4.8%
findings.quote: Blackpool Council rents are currently the 11th lowest in the country with 65% of rents set below formula rents.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3a Blackpool Council Rent Setting Policy 2026 , item 3.
findings.headline: Blackpool Council states it is committed to setting Affordable Rents below Local Housing Allowance rates.
findings.detail: The policy says this commitment sits outside the Government's Policy Statement and is intended to make properties affordable to local residents. Affordable Rents must also not exceed 80% of gross market rent under the Government's rules. The paper says Affordable Rent will normally only be used for new builds and acquisitions, not on re-let of existing stock.
findings.matters: Setting rents below the LHA ceiling limits the income an affordable-rent scheme can earn, which bears on the viability case for new supply at other councils.
findings.figures: Affordable Rent no more than 80% of gross market rent
findings.quote: Blackpool Council is committed to setting Affordable Rents below Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3a Blackpool Council Rent Setting Policy 2026 , item 3.
findings.headline: The policy retains a minimum HRA reserves level of £1 million.
findings.detail: The policy lists the retention of the previously agreed minimum reserves level as one of its purposes, to keep prudent balances in the HRA. The paper describes this as an existing agreed level, not a new one.
findings.matters: A stated minimum HRA reserve is the floor a finance director and lenders would test against the business plan.
findings.figures: £1 million minimum reserves level
findings.quote: Retain the previously agreed minimum reserves level of £1 million

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3a Blackpool Council Rent Setting Policy 2026 , item 3.
findings.headline: 85% of Blackpool Council's owned social housing stock was let below formula rent as of August 2025.
findings.detail: The policy describes re-evaluating rents when properties become vacant as essential to managing and maintaining the stock. It links that re-evaluation to the Council's regulatory responsibilities. Rents are to be set at formula rent on re-let, and convergence applies from April 2027.
findings.matters: The size of the gap between actual and formula rent is the main lever on HRA income over the 30-year business plan, and the share below formula rent shows how much headroom exists.
findings.figures: 85% of owned social housing stock let below formula rent, as of August 2025
findings.quote: As of August 2025, 85% of Blackpool Council’s owned social housing stock, are let below formula rent.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3a Blackpool Council Rent Setting Policy 2026 , item 3.
findings.headline: Blackpool's policy applies rent convergence of £1 a week from April 2027 and £2 a week from April 2028 on social rents below formula rent.
findings.detail: Rent convergence allows social rents below formula rent to rise by an amount over and above the CPI+1% limit until they reach formula rent. The policy sets the additional amount at £1 a week from April 2027, rising to £2 a week from April 2028. Section 3.7 says the Government announced in January 2026 that it intended to re-introduce convergence from April 2027.
findings.matters: A fixed weekly uplift on every below-formula property changes HRA rental income from 2027, and other councils with similar rent gaps will be modelling the same policy change.
findings.figures: £1 per week from April 2027; £2 per week from April 2028; CPI+1%
findings.quote: An additional £1 per week will be applied from April 2027, increasing to £2 per week from April 2028, until the formula rent is reached.

findings.headline: 80% of Blackpool Coastal Housing tenants are in receipt of benefits
findings.detail: The paper says that because most tenants receive benefits, rent increases will for the most part not affect them. It also notes that an equality analysis found no disproportionate adverse impact on protected groups.
findings.matters: The share of tenants whose rent is paid through benefits shapes HRA rent collection exposure, which a lender or peer council would take into account when assessing rent income.
findings.figures: 80% of Blackpool Coastal Housing tenants are in receipt of benefits
findings.quote: The majority (80%) of Blackpool Coastal Housing tenants are in receipt of benefits

findings.headline: Average Council social tenancy rent is projected to rise from £87.19 to £91.37 with the CPI+1 annual increase, and to £92.37 with rent convergence
findings.detail: The paper gives the projected average weekly rent after the annual increase and after the convergence increase. It describes the annual increase as based on CPI+1, currently 4.8%.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the projected rent uplift with HRA income assumptions and with the rent levels of neighbouring councils and registered providers.
findings.figures: £87.19 (2025/26 average weekly general rent); £91.37 annual rent increase (based on CPI+1 – currently 4.8%); £92.37 rent convergence rent increase (based on CPI+1 and an additional £1)
findings.quote: £91.37 Annual rent increase (based on CPI+1 – currently 4.8%)

findings.headline: Blackpool Council intends to use the full range of rent-setting options to align social rents to formula rent, including CPI+1 annual increases and rent flexibility
findings.detail: The paper lists the options the council will use: setting rents at formula rent on re-let, convergence where rents are below formula, annual increases of CPI+1, and rent flexibility where there is a clear rationale. The paper says this is to keep the HRA financially viable and the stock in good condition.
findings.matters: It shows the council's chosen approach to raising HRA rent income over the policy period, which a lender or peer council can weigh against its own rent-setting strategy.
findings.figures: Policy in effect until 1 April 2028; CPI currently 4.8% (CPI+1 basis as stated in the paper)
findings.quote: Blackpool Council intends to utilise the full range of options available to them to align social rents to Formula Rent

findings.headline: 65% of Council properties are rented below formula rent, and the policy adopts rent convergence of an additional £1 a week from April 2027 and £2 a week from April 2028
findings.detail: The paper says the Government intends to re-introduce rent convergence from April 2027, allowing landlords to add £1 a week, and from April 2028 £2 a week, to normal increases where rents are below formula rent. The policy is set to use convergence where rents are below formula rent.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council or a lender can compare how much rent headroom the HRA has against formula rent, which sets the income base for debt service and stock investment.
findings.figures: 65% of Council properties are currently rented below formula rent; an additional £1 a week from April 2027 and an additional £2 a week from April 2028
findings.quote: 65% of Council properties are currently rented below formula rent.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4a Heritage Investment Strategy Final , item 4.
findings.headline: The Heritage Programme Board "will not replace existing governance arrangements or act as a grant-making body."
findings.detail: The paper states that expenditure, procurement and investment approvals remain subject to the relevant organisational processes. It also describes investment as broadly defined, including advice, advocacy and help securing external funding, alongside direct financial investment.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know that the strategy's main body commits no grant money of its own and that spending still runs through existing approvals, since the paper sets out no funding amount.
findings.figures: No funding amounts given.
findings.quote: The Board will not replace existing governance arrangements or act as a grant-making body.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4a Heritage Investment Strategy Final , item 4.
findings.headline: The strategy cites Local Government Reorganisation in Lancashire as a transition that heritage planning must account for.
findings.detail: The paper says the transition 'creates an important moment to establish a clear direction for heritage in Blackpool'. It adds that the delivery framework is intended to respond to potential changes from local government reorganisation.
findings.matters: Reorganisation changes the councils, boundaries and budgets that heritage spending depends on, which matters to finance officers at Blackpool and at other councils going through the same process.
findings.figures: No figures given.
findings.quote: The transition associated with Local Government Reorganisation in Lancashire also creates an important moment to establish a clear direction for heritage in Blackpool.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4a Heritage Investment Strategy Final , item 4.
findings.headline: Blackpool Council owns around 25% of all listed and locally listed buildings in the town, including Blackpool Tower and the Winter Gardens.
findings.detail: The paper says these council-owned assets 'require substantial ongoing investment and care'. It also says the future of the town's heritage depends equally on buildings owned privately, by businesses, charities and communities.
findings.matters: A council holding a quarter of the town's listed and locally listed buildings carries a large, ongoing maintenance and conservation liability that a finance director needs to plan for, and peers with heritage estates face the same exposure.
findings.figures: "around 25%" of all listed and locally listed buildings in the town. The paper gives no cost figure for the investment required.
findings.quote: These assets require substantial ongoing investment and care.

findings.headline: Council states rent increases are necessary to ensure Housing Revenue Account financial viability and meet regulatory requirements
findings.detail: Blackpool Council is adopting a rent setting policy including annual CPI+1 increases, rent convergence (an additional £1 per week from April 2027 and £2 per week from April 2028 when rents are below formula rent), and rent flexibility for new tenants. The council cites 'significant financial challenges' in meeting housing obligations and maintaining safe, well-maintained stock, explicitly stating that 'failure to set rents at the appropriate level will impact on our ability to provide homes that meet Regulatory requirements'. Currently 65% of properties are rented below formula rent.
findings.matters: A council explicitly acknowledging that a major ringfenced service faces financial constraint and requires rent increases to meet regulatory obligations and service debt is material to lenders and finance officers assessing the council's overall financial position.
findings.figures: Current average rents £87.19 (general rent) and £115.05 (affordable rent); 65% of properties rented below formula rent; projected average increase to £91.37 with CPI+1 or £92.37 with rent convergence; 80% of tenants in receipt of benefits
findings.quote: There are significant financial challenges faced in meeting housing obligations, complying with regulatory standards, and guaranteeing our homes are safe and well-maintained. Re-evaluating rents is critical to ensuring that we are able to manage and maintain our stock in line with our regulatory responsibilities.

findings.headline: After increases, Blackpool's social rents remain 11th lowest nationally and significantly below North West regional average.
findings.detail: Proposed increases place Blackpool's average social rent at £91.37-£92.37 per week. The council notes this 'still places Blackpool Council rents considerably below the rest of the North West and the neighbouring areas of Wyres and Fylde'. Regional comparators: North West average £100.51, Wyre £102.70, Fylde £107.41. Current Blackpool rents rank 11th lowest in England.
findings.matters: The extent of rental increase headroom affects the adequacy of the rent policy and HRA financial sustainability; a finance director would note Blackpool retains capacity for future increases while remaining competitive with regional peers.
findings.figures: £91.37 (CPI+1); £92.37 (with convergence); North West £100.51, Wyre £102.70, Fylde £107.41; nationally 11th lowest
findings.quote: This still places Blackpool Council rents considerably below the rest of the North West and the neighbouring areas of Wyres and Fylde. As such the proposed increases, while impacting on expendable income of some residents, will not result in properties becoming unaffordable

findings.headline: 80% of council tenants receive housing benefits, insulating majority from disposable income impact of rent increases.
findings.detail: The document notes that 80% of BCH tenants are in receipt of benefits that cover their rent. For these tenants, increases are paid through Housing Support allowances and do not reduce disposable income. The council cites government impact assessment confirming that 'Tenants who are in receipt of Housing Support benefits will not experience the same impact as those who pay their own rent'.
findings.matters: The real financial impact of rent increases on household budgets is less severe than headline figures suggest when most tenants are protected by housing allowances; this affects affordability concerns and risk of arrears or collection problems.
findings.figures: 80% of BCH tenants on benefits; subgroups show 75-85% on benefits by protected characteristic
findings.quote: The majority (80%) of BCH tenants are in receipt of benefits and will therefore, for the most part, not be directly impacted by proposed rent increases.

findings.headline: Tenant consultation (June-September 2026) on rent increases generated zero concerns as of decision date, suggesting acceptance or indifference.
findings.detail: The council published a consultation on 10 June 2026 with information on impact, amounts, and rationale. As of 2 September 2026—three months into the consultation period—the council reports receiving no tenant contact expressing concerns. The council states this 'provides us with some assurance that tenants are not unduly concerned about the rent increases'. The Executive will vote on the policy on 12 October 2026.
findings.matters: Implementation risk for rent increases depends partly on tenant acceptance; the absence of concerns over three months suggests either positive reception or lack of mobilised opposition, improving feasibility of the policy change.
findings.figures: Consultation published 10 June 2026; zero concerns received as of 2 September 2026; Executive decision meeting 12 October 2026
findings.quote: As of 2nd September 2026, we have not received any contact from tenants expressing concerns regarding rent changes which provides us with some assurance that tenants are not unduly concerned about the rent increases.

findings.headline: Council approved rent increases at end of 2025/26 to close HRA revenue gap; 65% of 4,624 tenanted properties currently set below formula rent level.
findings.detail: The council identified that current rental income is insufficient to fund maintenance, building safety compliance, decarbonisation, and new investment. Approximately 65% of properties are set below formula rent, which the council states 'significantly limits rental income'. The council approved the policy 'on the grounds that failure to do so would result in an inability to generate the necessary investment in our existing council housing stock, steps towards decarbonisation, and investment in new Council homes'. Increasing regulatory requirements for disrepair compliance are cited as a key driver.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand whether HRA revenue is adequate for maintenance and investment obligations; this shows a material funding gap the council is addressing through rent policy reform.
findings.figures: 65% of rents below formula rent; 4,624 tenanted properties; average rent £87.19/week (2025/26), rising to £91.37-£92.37 after increases; formula rent convergence of £1-2 per week
findings.quote: approximately 65% of BCH rents are set below formula rents, which significantly limits rental income. As the regulatory environment changes and new, more stringent, requirements for addressing disrepair is prescribed, failure to maximise budgets will significantly impact on how we can deliver on our responsibilities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3a Blackpool Council Rent Setting Policy 2026
findings.headline: Council expects benefit rises to cover rent increases for approximately 70% of tenants.
findings.detail: The policy states an expectation that 'the majority of tenants (approx. 70%) will have rent increases covered by benefit rises.' This is a key affordability assumption underpinning the rent increase strategy, which includes CPI+1% annual increases plus Rent Convergence additions from April 2027.
findings.matters: This assumption about welfare indexation is critical to assessing the real affordability impact of above-inflation rent increases on the tenant base. If benefit increases fall short, more tenants will face affordability pressures, potentially affecting rent arrears and collection. A finance director would want to test whether this assumption holds in practice.
findings.figures: 70% of tenants
findings.quote: Our expectation is that the majority of tenants (approx. 70%) will have rent increases covered by benefit rises.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3a Blackpool Council Rent Setting Policy 2026
findings.headline: HRA policy targets minimum reserves of £1 million.
findings.detail: The rent setting policy commits to maintaining a minimum reserve level of £1 million in the HRA, described as a 'previously agreed' target intended to ensure 'prudent balances are maintained in the HRA'.
findings.matters: Reserve policy indicates financial prudence and resilience in a ring-fenced account. A lender assesses HRA financial health partly through reserve adequacy, and a finance director at another council would want to know how peers balance reserves against capital investment demands.
findings.figures: £1 million minimum
findings.quote: Retain the previously agreed minimum reserves level of £1 million to ensure that prudent balances are maintained in the HRA.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3a Blackpool Council Rent Setting Policy 2026
findings.headline: 85% of Blackpool Council's owned social housing stock let below formula rent as of August 2025; Rent Convergence from April 2027 to add £1–£2 per week above CPI+1% annual increase.
findings.detail: As of August 2025, 85% of Blackpool Council's stock was let below government formula rent levels. From April 2027, government policy allows councils to apply additional weekly increases (£1 per week from April 2027, rising to £2 per week from April 2028) on top of the standard CPI+1% annual increase until rents converge with formula rent. The council intends to use this mechanism alongside re-let uplifts to bring its stock into alignment.
findings.matters: This reveals a material opportunity to increase HRA income from the majority of the council's stock over the next two to three years, essential to HRA viability given the 30-year business plan and maintenance commitments. A lender would want to track whether this income improvement materializes as planned.
findings.figures: 85% of stock below formula rent as of August 2025; £1 per week from April 2027, increasing to £2 per week from April 2028
findings.quote: As of August 2025, 85% of Blackpool Council's owned social housing stock, are let below formula rent. As such, re-evaluating rents when properties become vacant is critical to ensuring that we are able to manage and maintain our stock in line with our regulatory responsibilities.

findings.headline: 80% of Blackpool Coastal Housing tenants are benefits-recipients, limiting direct financial impact of proposed rent increases
findings.detail: Equality analysis found no disproportionate adverse impacts on protected characteristics. Council provides support for tenants managing increases including drop-in centres, extended opening hours, dedicated Financial Services Officers, and income maximization support. Rent Flexibility (above formula rent) applies only to new/incoming tenants with assessments and support available at point of allocation.
findings.matters: Benefits-funding of rents reduces rent collection risk and uncollectable arrears exposure from increase implementation
findings.figures: 80% of BCH tenants on benefits
findings.quote: The majority (80%) of Blackpool Coastal Housing tenants are in receipt of benefits (including older people and those on disability related benefits) and will therefore, for the most part, not be impacted by proposed rent increases.

findings.headline: Council adopting comprehensive rent-setting policy applying CPI+1 annually, Rent Convergence, and Rent Flexibility to ensure Housing Revenue Account financial viability
findings.detail: Policy approved for effect until 1 April 2028. Council will set rents at formula rent on vacant re-lets, apply Rent Convergence when applicable, increase rents annually by CPI+1, and apply Rent Flexibility (above formula rent) where local rationale exists. Paper states that failure to set rents appropriately will impact the council's ability to maintain homes to regulatory standards.
findings.matters: Financial viability of the HRA is essential to service housing debt and maintain stock condition; this shows explicit council commitment to use available tools
findings.figures: Policy term until 1 April 2028
findings.quote: Blackpool Council intends to utilise the full range of options available to them to align social rents to Formula Rent, to ensure that the Housing Revenue Account remains finically viable and to ensure that the quality and condition of stock remains high.

findings.headline: Blackpool social rents average £87.19/week (11th lowest in England), providing headroom to increase toward formula rent while remaining below regional average of £100.51
findings.detail: Current average weekly rent £87.19 for general properties. CPI+1 increase (currently 4.8%) would raise this to £91.37/week, or £92.37 with rent convergence. This remains materially below the North West average of £100.51 and national average of £113.69, indicating capacity to increase further.
findings.matters: Shows the financial headroom available to a council for HRA revenue improvement without pricing rents above regional comparators
findings.figures: Current: £87.19/week; CPI+1: £91.37/week; with convergence: £92.37/week; North West average: £100.51; national average: £113.69; ranked 11th lowest nationally
findings.quote: Blackpool Council rents are currently the 11th lowest in the country with 65% of rents set below formula rents. In 2025/26 the average weekly rent charged in Blackpool was £87.19 for general rent properties and £115.05 for affordable rent properties, so tenants will enjoy low rents despite increases.

findings.headline: Government re-introduced Rent Convergence from April 2027 enabling additional £1/week increases, and from April 2028 additional £2/week, with 65% of Blackpool properties qualifying
findings.detail: Blackpool Council intends to use the full range of rent-setting tools available under the 2026 Rent Standard, including Rent Convergence which allows increases above the standard CPI+1 when rents are below formula rent. Since 65% of Council properties are currently below formula rent, the authority has substantial capacity to increase housing revenue over the convergence period.
findings.matters: This is a new external source of permission for HRA revenue growth; how councils deploy it shapes their housing debt servicing capacity and investment capability
findings.figures: 65% of properties below formula rent; additional £1/week from April 2027, £2/week from April 2028
findings.quote: In January, 2026 the Government announced its intention to re-introduce Rent Convergence from April 2027, which allows landlords to increase rents by an additional £1 a week and from April 2028 an additional £2 a week, above normal rent increases when rents are below formula rent. 65% of Council properties are currently rented below formula rent.

findings.headline: DSG deficit of £7.331m to be 90% written off by High Needs Stability Grant, leaving council to fund 10%
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant Reserve held a deficit of £7.331m as at 31 March 2026. The Department for Education's High Needs Stability Grant will write off 90% of this accrued deficit, leaving the Council responsible for managing and funding the remaining 10% (approximately £733k). Future deficits accrued in 2026/27 onwards may be covered by future HNSG payments, but this is not yet confirmed by DfE as their review of High Needs funding continues.
findings.matters: Partial bailout masks underlying structural high-needs funding gap; future DSG deficits uncertain and could resume accumulating if HNSG support is not confirmed
findings.figures: £7,331k DSG deficit at 31 March 2026; 90% written off by HNSG; Council responsible for £733k; future HNSG payments not yet confirmed
findings.quote: This one-off Grant will write-off 90% of the accrued DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026, with the Council responsible for managing and funding the remaining 10%. Deficits accrued in 2026/27 and beyond may be covered by future HNSG payments, but this is yet to be confirmed by the DfE

findings.headline: Asset Disposal Plan is critical to financial position, required to cover £6.663m Growth & Prosperity and £4.966m Flexible Use of Capital Receipts targets
findings.detail: Forecast Earmarked Revenue Reserves of £21.34m assume that in-year Growth & Prosperity deficit (£6.663m) and Flexible Use of Capital Receipts target (£4.966m) are covered by the Asset Disposal Plan. An Asset Disposal working group has been established, meeting monthly, and is developing a contingency plan to mitigate delivery risk. Total of £11.6m in required disposals underpins the current financial forecast.
findings.matters: Primary mechanism for balancing the position depends on achieving significant asset sales; failure to deliver disposals would immediately create £11.6m financing gap
findings.figures: £6,663k G&P overspend dependent on Asset Disposal; £4,966k Flexible Use of Capital Receipts dependent on Asset Disposal; total £11.629m
findings.quote: This figure also assumes the in-year Growth & Prosperity (£6.663m) and the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts target (£4.966m) are covered by the Asset Disposal Plan. An Asset Disposal working group has been set up and is meeting monthly to progress these disposals

findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate at 26% at month 3, 3rd lowest in England; CTRS collection at 20.8%
findings.detail: Being the most deprived local authority in England, Council Tax collection is identified as a challenge. The 2025/26 collection rate dipped from 4th lowest to 3rd lowest in England. At end month 3, £21.8m collected at 26% collection rate. Cumulative collection on arrears (2020/21 to 2025/26) at 91.4%. The Council Tax Reduction Scheme collection is under 'similar pressure' due to accumulated arrears and cost of living impact on household income.
findings.matters: Weak collection rates on main revenue source, with accumulated arrears and cost-of-living pressures suggesting continued headwinds to income recovery
findings.figures: 26.0% collection rate at month 3; 3rd lowest in England for 2025/26; cumulative arrears collection rate 91.4%; CTRS collection rate 20.8%
findings.quote: Being the most deprived local authority in England per the Office for National Statistics, collection of Council Tax is a challenge and 2025/26 saw the collection rate dip from 4th lowest in England to 3rd lowest

findings.headline: Council borrowing nearly doubled from £250m (2017/18) to £587m (2025/26) with 50:50 split between long and short-term at rates exceeding 6%
findings.detail: Council borrowing has grown from less than £250m at end 2017/18 to £587m at end 2025/26, forecast to £605m. The borrowing profile changed to 50:50 long-term and short-term split as at 2025/26, after shorter 'long-term' borrowing was taken in 2025/26. Long-term PWLB rates currently exceed 6% despite base rate at 3.75%. Month 3 2026/27 shows long-term borrowing increased by £28.4m.
findings.matters: Doubling of borrowing stock combined with elevated long-term rates and shift to shorter-term debt increases refinancing and interest rate risk exposure
findings.figures: £587m at 2025/26; forecast £605m for 2026/27; long-term rates >6%; short-term borrowing increased £28.4m in first 3 months
findings.quote: Council borrowing has doubled from less than £250m at the end of 2017/18 to £587m at the end of 2025/26. The profile of this borrowing has also changed to a 50:50 split of long-term and short-term borrowing as at 2025/26

findings.headline: Strategic Leisure Assets (Tower and Winter Gardens) forecast £1.721m overspend with cumulative deficit expected to reach £12.474m
findings.detail: Strategic Leisure Assets is forecasting a £1.721m pressure in 2026/27. Cumulative deficit expected to reach £12.474m by 31 March 2027. The council notes that under the original 2011 Executive decision, any over/underspend is transferred to an Earmarked Reserve. A new leisure assets medium-term financial plan is being worked up following management change (creation of Blackpool Tourism Limited). The previous plan expected to break-even cumulatively by 2034/35.
findings.matters: Long-term cultural/tourism investment with significant accumulated deficit and uncertain breakeven timeline; dependent on Blackpool Tourism Limited's commercial performance
findings.figures: £1,721k forecast pressure; £12,474k cumulative deficit forecast at 31 March 2027; previous MTFP expected breakeven by 2034/35
findings.quote: Strategic Leisure Assets, which largely relates to the investment in key historic and economic assets of Blackpool Tower and the Winter Gardens, forecast a pressure of £1,721k... cumulative deficit as at 31 March 2027 will be £12,474k

findings.headline: Growth and Prosperity schemes creating £8.049m in-year pressure with cumulative deficit forecast at £10.273m
findings.detail: Growth and Prosperity schemes are forecasting an £8.049m pressure (£6.663m from schemes, £1.386m from Enterprise Zone). Cumulative deficit at 31 March 2027 expected to be £10.273m for Growth & Prosperity and £2.166m for Enterprise Zone. The council notes this is treated as 'nil' variance as it assumes the in-year deficit will be covered by the Asset Disposal Plan. These investments are described as having 'long term financial payback' but create 'short to medium term challenge'.
findings.matters: Major speculative investment in jobs and economic regeneration is accumulating deficits dependent on asset sales; delivery risk on disposal plan threatens consolidated position
findings.figures: £8,049k pressure; £10,273k cumulative deficit G&P; £2,166k cumulative deficit Enterprise Zone
findings.quote: The service is forecasting a £8,049k pressure which is made up of £6,663k from Growth & Prosperity schemes and £1,386k from the Enterprise Zone... This investment in jobs and the economy, in projects such as the Civil Service Hub and Enterprise Zone infrastructure, presents a short to medium term challenge, with long term financial payback

findings.headline: Earmarked Revenue Reserves forecast to decline from £27.2m to £21.3m in-year, then to £14.7m by March 2028
findings.detail: At 31 March 2026, Earmarked Revenue Reserves stood at £27.185m. The forecast shows decline to £21.34m by 31 March 2027 and further to £14.7m by 31 March 2028. Key drawdowns include £6.663m from Growth and Prosperity reserve, £1.721m from Strategic Leisure Assets, and £1.386m from Enterprise Zone, assuming Asset Disposal Plan delivers as expected.
findings.matters: Multi-year reserve depletion trajectory shows the council is funding current operations partly from reserves and special initiatives; unsustainable without new revenue sources
findings.figures: £27.185m at 1 April 2026; forecast £21.34m at 31 March 2027; forecast £14.7m at 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Earmarked Revenue Reserves (ERR) as at 31 March 2026 are £27.185m, however, these are forecast to reduce to £21.340m by 31 March 2027

findings.headline: Children's Social Care placements forecast £4.2m overspend driven by residential placements at 78 against capacity
findings.detail: Residential placements are at 78 as at 30 June 2026, forecast to reduce to 64 by 31 March 2027. The council reports 531 children in care (188 per 10,000 population 0-17), higher than statistical neighbours will be post-Local Government Reforms. Residential care unit costs and volumes are the two largest drivers of the budget pressure. The council is using Care Cubed benchmarking tool to negotiate with providers and working to step children into lower-cost foster care and semi-independent settings.
findings.matters: Structural demand pressure on a statutory service with no capacity to underspend; residential placement rates above national average reflect service complexity and cost exposure
findings.figures: £4,203k forecast overspend; 78 residential placements (forecast 64); 531 children in care; £3,384k of the overspend from placements
findings.quote: Children's Social Care Placements are forecasting an overspend of £3,384k, mainly due to new-to-care placements being higher than those exiting care and the additional support required following the breakdown of high-cost placements

findings.headline: Working balances forecast to fall to £2.08m against a £7.8m target, leaving minimal headroom
findings.detail: The Council set a target of £7.8m working balances by 31 March 2027 but is forecasting only £2.08m after accounting for a £6.9m budgeted transfer at the start of the year. This represents a sharp decline from historic levels and leaves the Council with very limited buffer for volatility or unexpected pressures.

findings.headline: Council is positioning debt portfolio to hedge interest rate risk, maintaining 50:50 split between long-term and short-term borrowing
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Panel has deliberately maintained a 50:50 split between long-term and short-term borrowing for 2026/27 to offset economic uncertainty. This is operationalised through active short-term money market management, with £204m received and £526m paid out in Q1 alone, against a full-year budget of £247m for payments.
findings.matters: This shows how the council is managing interest rate risk in an uncertain environment. The deliberate portfolio positioning, combined with active short-term operations, indicates thoughtful treasury stewardship. findings.matters: Demand drivers imposed by external policy (NHS discharge protocols) can create persistent budget pressure that the council cannot eliminate by efficiency alone. Understanding this is essential to assess whether the overspend will continue and requires structural budget change.

findings.matters: Unachieved savings signal either overly optimistic budget assumptions or barriers to planned service efficiencies. This matters for assessing whether the overspend is temporary variance or a sign of structural issues with budget forecasting or service delivery.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3p M3 2627 Directorate Budget Savings Performance
findings.headline: Transformation programs expected to deliver multi-year returns while council cannot deliver baseline recurring savings, creating compounding budget risk
findings.detail: Blackpool's transformation programs are expected to deliver returns over 2026/27–2028/29, but their success is uncertain and benefits typically materialize slower than planned. The council is simultaneously failing to achieve its baseline recurring savings target. If transformation programs slip or deliver returns below forecast, the council has no buffer of achieved recurrent savings to absorb the slippage.
findings.matters: A council betting on transformation ROI while unable to hit baseline savings targets is doubly exposed to budget deterioration. Any program slippage or capital receipts shortfall could trigger a funding crisis within 12 months.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3p M3 2627 Directorate Budget Savings Performance
findings.headline: Council is using finite capital receipts (£11.2m deployed) to fund transformation programs instead of delivering recurrent savings—the £1.2m savings shortfall matches exactly the remaining capital receipts not yet deployed
findings.detail: Blackpool is using "Flexible Use of Capital Receipts" to finance transformation investments (Digital Transformation £1,127k; Early Help £2,358k; Ofsted improvement £183k; CQC improvement £566k; Adults Commissioning £429k; Financial Systems £243k). As at 30 June, £11,243k of £12,466k total planned capital receipts has been deployed, leaving £1,223k—which exactly matches the council's unachievable recurrent savings shortfall. This approach funds ongoing commitments from one-off asset sale proceeds that may not be repeated.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts to mask a recurring revenue budget deficit is not sustainable. If capital receipts dry up or asset sales slow, the council loses its funding source for transformation investments while the underlying revenue problem persists. This creates acute vulnerability.
findings.figures: Capital receipts deployment: £11,243k of £12,466k as at 30 June; transformation investments of £4,966k (2026/27) and £5,065k (2027/28); outstanding capital receipts of £1,223k exactly equals the unachievable recurrent savings gap.
findings.quote: As at 30 June 2026 it is forecast that £11,243k of the £12.466m saving has been delivered. Work continues to deliver the original proposals as well as alternatives if they are unachievable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3p M3 2627 Directorate Budget Savings Performance
findings.headline: Only £1.4m of £7.5m recurrent savings achieved; £1.2m marked unachievable and £1.8m not yet found, with 100% of Children's Services target unachievable
findings.detail: As at 30 June 2026, Blackpool has achieved only £1,392k of its £7,500k savings target (18.6%). The council expects to deliver a further £4,885k by year-end, totalling £6,277k. However, £1,223k is explicitly marked "not able to be achieved" and £1,823k is "not yet found recurrently". Shortfalls are concentrated: Children's Services cannot achieve any of its £1,000k target (achieved £0k); Chief Executive cannot achieve £450k of £1,795k; Corporate cannot achieve £273k of £2,000k; Place has not identified £500k.
findings.matters: A council that cannot deliver planned savings must close the gap through borrowing, reserve drawdowns, or unplanned service reductions. The concentration of unachievable cuts in children's and corporate services suggests structural problems in those areas that will worsen over time.
